scenes.visual: Title card 'Reading Evolution Across Time' over a row of freezer vials. Same colour map as the first film. COLOUR MAP, same in both films: plant/host GREEN; fungus/parasite/phage PURPLE; rhizobia GOLD; benefit block TEAL; cost block RED; net bar GREY on a scale marked +, 0, -; rotifer ORANGE; alga GREEN. Cream background, 16:9. Numbers appear only as on-screen text. Cartoons and labelled blocks only, no molecular structures; anything not computed is labelled 'schematic'.

scenes.tts: The first film scored each partner's side as a net. When both partners evolve, each resets the other's net. How can you see that?
scenes.visual: Brief recap: the first film's two linked balances (GREEN host, PURPLE partner) tilt back and forth. A clock appears above them, then the question 'how do you see it?'.
scenes.narration: The first film scored each partner's side as a net. When both partners evolve, each resets the other's net. How can you see that?

scenes.tts: Take a bacterium and a phage, a virus that infects bacteria. Freeze samples of both every two weeks, to revive later.
scenes.visual: A timeline across the screen labelled 'weeks' 0 to 20. At every second week a GREEN vial (host) and a PURPLE vial (phage) drop into a freezer rack beneath the timeline.
scenes.narration: Take a bacterium and a phage, a virus that infects bacteria. Freeze samples of both every two weeks, to revive later.

scenes.tts: Now cross them in a time-shift assay. Phages from one time meet hosts from the past, the same time and the future.
scenes.visual: A grid: rows 'phage from week', columns 'host from week'. The PURPLE week-10 vial slides out and lines connect it to GREEN vials from weeks 4, 10 and 16, labelled 'past', 'same time', 'future'.
scenes.narration: Now cross them in a time-shift assay. Phages from one time meet hosts from the past, the same time and the future.

scenes.tts: If neither partner's heritable traits changed, every pairing should give about the same infection rate. A repeatable difference means at least one partner changed. The shape hints at how.
scenes.visual: Three bars for the three pairings stand at equal height, labelled 'no heritable change'. Then they move apart, with small error bars, and the label changes to 'at least one partner changed'. An empty axis appears: x 'time gap: host minus phage', with '- past hosts' at the left, '0 same time' in the middle and '+ future hosts' at the right; y 'infection'.
scenes.narration: If neither partner's heritable traits changed, every pairing should give about the same infection rate. A repeatable difference means at least one partner changed. The shape hints at how.

scenes.tts: First, an arms race. Host resistance and phage infectivity both rise, in repeated rounds.
scenes.visual: Two staircases climb side by side, GREEN 'host resistance' and PURPLE 'phage infectivity', each step a round. Schematic.
scenes.narration: First, an arms race. Host resistance and phage infectivity both rise, in repeated rounds.

scenes.tts: Take one phage from the middle of the series. Test it on past, same-time and future hosts. Which does it infect best?
scenes.visual: The three pairings from the grid return, with three empty bars marked 'week 4', 'week 10', 'week 16' and a question mark. A PURPLE tag reads 'phage from week 10'.
scenes.narration: Take one phage from the middle of the series. Test it on past, same-time and future hosts. Which does it infect best?

scenes.visual: Hold the three empty bars and the question mark; a countdown ring fills.

scenes.tts: The past hosts. This phage has never met the resistance that later hosts evolved. Infection falls from past hosts to future ones, and keeps falling as the gap grows.
scenes.visual: The bars fill: tallest at week 4, shortest at week 16; a small tag on the week-16 bar reads 'resistance this phage has not met'. Then the infection axis returns and a PURPLE line draws a steady downward slope from the past-hosts side to the future-hosts side, labelled 'arms race: one-way trend' (computed from a toy model).
scenes.narration: The past hosts. This phage has never met the resistance that later hosts evolved. Infection falls from past hosts to future ones, and keeps falling as the gap grows.

scenes.tts: Fluctuating selection works differently. Whichever host type is common gets attacked most. Rare types then gain, and the advantage keeps shifting.
scenes.visual: A GREEN host population of two shapes, circles and squares. PURPLE phages swarm the commoner shape; it dwindles and the other shape becomes common; the phages switch. Repeat once.
scenes.narration: Fluctuating selection works differently. Whichever host type is common gets attacked most. Rare types then gain, and the advantage keeps shifting.

scenes.tts: Phages track the common host type, so they tend to do best on hosts of about their own time. As the gap grows, infection rises and falls, with no long-run trend.
scenes.visual: On the infection axis, a second PURPLE curve draws in as a wave across a wide time-gap axis, its highest point at or near zero (same time), labelled 'fluctuating selection: rises and falls, no trend' (computed from a two-type host-parasite model).
scenes.narration: Phages track the common host type, so they tend to do best on hosts of about their own time. As the gap grows, infection rises and falls, with no long-run trend.

scenes.tts: So read the shape as evidence, not proof. A one-way trend points to escalation. A wave with no long-run trend points to tracking.
scenes.visual: Both curves on one axis, the straight slope and the wave, with labels 'points to escalation' and 'points to tracking', and a small caption 'evidence, not proof'.
scenes.narration: So read the shape as evidence, not proof. A one-way trend points to escalation. A wave with no long-run trend points to tracking.

scenes.tts: Evolution can also act within a population cycle. Picture a chemostat, a vessel with a steady inflow and a matching outflow. Rotifers graze on algae.
scenes.visual: A glass vessel with an inflow tube and an outflow tube. GREEN algal cells and ORANGE rotifer cartoons swim inside; rotifers eat algae.
scenes.narration: Evolution can also act within a population cycle. Picture a chemostat, a vessel with a steady inflow and a matching outflow. Rotifers graze on algae.

scenes.tts: In classical models, prey rise, predators multiply, prey crash, predators starve. Rotifer peaks trail algal peaks by about a quarter cycle. That delay, as a fraction of the period, is the phase lag.
scenes.visual: Two traces over time, GREEN algae and ORANGE rotifers, each a smooth wave; small arrows mark 'prey rise', 'predators multiply', 'prey crash', 'predators starve'. The ORANGE peak sits a quarter of the period after the GREEN peak. A bracket marks 'delay' and another marks 'period'; text 'phase lag = delay / period' and 'about 0.25 in the classical case'. Schematic.
scenes.narration: In classical models, prey rise, predators multiply, prey crash, predators starve. Rotifer peaks trail algal peaks by about a quarter cycle. That delay, as a fraction of the period, is the phase lag.

scenes.tts: Takehito Yoshida and colleagues started the algae in two ways. A clone is a set of genetically identical cells. One clone cannot evolve by selection among clones. Several clones can.
scenes.visual: Two vessels: left labelled 'one clone (identical cells)' with identical GREEN cells; right labelled 'several clones' with GREEN cells in several shades.
scenes.narration: Takehito Yoshida and colleagues started the algae in two ways. A clone is a set of genetically identical cells. One clone cannot evolve by selection among clones. Several clones can.

scenes.tts: One clone gave short cycles, close to the quarter lag. Several clones gave long cycles, with rotifer and algal peaks largely out of step.
scenes.visual: Under each vessel, GREEN and ORANGE traces. Left: short cycles, peaks a quarter cycle apart. Right: long cycles, ORANGE peaks near the GREEN troughs, labelled 'largely out of step'. Schematic.
scenes.narration: One clone gave short cycles, close to the quarter lag. Several clones gave long cycles, with rotifer and algal peaks largely out of step.

scenes.tts: The algae carry their own balance. Defence against grazing costs them in nutrient competition. Many rotifers favour defence. Few rotifers favour fast growth.
scenes.visual: A small balance for a defended GREEN alga: TEAL block 'escape from grazing', RED block 'poorer nutrient competition'. As ORANGE rotifer numbers rise the balance tips to TEAL; as they fall it tips to RED. Schematic.
scenes.narration: The algae carry their own balance. Defence against grazing costs them in nutrient competition. Many rotifers favour defence. Few rotifers favour fast growth.

scenes.tts: These runs showed prey evolution changing population cycles. Predator evolution was not tested. So this is eco-evolutionary feedback, not shown coevolution.
scenes.visual: The GREEN alga gets a tick labelled 'evolved'; the ORANGE rotifer gets a grey label 'not tested'. A loop of two arrows: 'evolution changes numbers' and 'numbers change selection'. Text: 'eco-evolutionary feedback'.
scenes.narration: These runs showed prey evolution changing population cycles. Predator evolution was not tested. So this is eco-evolutionary feedback, not shown coevolution.

scenes.tts: Pairing partners from different times reveals change. A trend points to escalation, a wave to tracking. Coevolution also needs heritable change in both partners, checked with controls.
scenes.visual: The freezer rack and the two curves from the time-shift assay return side by side; the slope and the wave pulse in turn. A third small panel shows a GREEN host and a PURPLE phage, each with a tag 'heritable change?', beside a smaller tag 'control: one side held fixed'.
scenes.narration: Pairing partners from different times reveals change. A trend points to escalation, a wave to tracking. Coevolution also needs heritable change in both partners, checked with controls.

scenes.visual: End card with the Hex mascot. One line only: 'Across time: a one-way trend points to escalation, a wave to tracking.'
